blocks.prompt: The Star We Live Next To
blocks.text: The sun looks small in the sky. It is not small. The sun is a giant ball of hot gas. It only looks small because it is so far away. If the sun were a hollow ball, you could pour more than a million Earths inside it. The sun is not on fire like a campfire. Deep inside, it squeezes tiny bits of gas together so hard that they make light and heat. That light flies across space for eight minutes and lands on your face. Every plant you have ever seen grew on sunlight. So did the food you ate today.

blocks.prompt: The Star We Live Next To
blocks.text: Go outside on a clear day and there is a star right above you. It is the only star you can see in daylight, and you have known its name your whole life. It is the sun. The sun is a star, exactly like the ones that come out at night. Those stars look like pinpricks because they are unimaginably far away. The sun looks huge because it is close. Close, for a star, still means 93 million miles. The sun is a ball of glowing gas about 109 times as wide as Earth. It is not burning the way wood burns in a fireplace. Deep in its core, gravity squeezes a gas called hydrogen so hard that it turns into a different gas called helium. Each time that happens, a small amount of energy escapes. It happens so often, and so fast, that the sun has been shining for four and a half billion years and is nowhere near finished. Sunlight takes about eight minutes and twenty seconds to cross the gap to Earth. When you watch the sun go down, you are seeing light that left it before you walked outside.

blocks.prompt: A Star Close Enough to Feel
blocks.text: Pick any star in the night sky. It is a huge ball of glowing gas, pouring out light in every direction, slowly working through its fuel. Now look at the sun. Same thing. The only real difference is the distance. That distance is 93 million miles, which sounds enormous until you compare it to the next star over. Sunlight reaches Earth in about eight minutes. Light from the next nearest star takes more than four years. The sun is about 865,000 miles across, roughly 109 times the width of Earth. It also holds about 99.8 percent of all the material in the solar system. Every planet, every moon, every comet and asteroid and speck of dust, all of it put together, is the leftovers. The sun is not burning the way a candle burns. Candles need oxygen, and there is no oxygen in space. The sun's energy comes from its core, where gravity presses hydrogen together so hard that the hydrogen fuses into helium. Fusing releases a staggering amount of energy, and it is why the sun has kept shining for four and a half billion years without running low. Its surface runs at about 10,000 degrees Fahrenheit. Dark patches called sunspots drift across it, appear for a few weeks, and fade. A sunspot looks black in a photograph, but it is not black. It is only cooler than the blazing gas around it, and next to that, cooler looks like dark. If you could lift one sunspot out and hang it alone in the night sky, it would glow brighter than the full moon.

blocks.prompt: The Star That Runs Everything
blocks.text: The sun is an ordinary star. Astronomers file it under yellow dwarf, which sounds like an insult and is not one. It is middling in size, middling in temperature, middling in age. There are stars far larger and far brighter, and plenty that are smaller and dimmer. What makes the sun extraordinary is not the sun. It is you, standing 93 million miles away, close enough to be warmed and far enough not to be cooked. Everything the sun does begins in its core. There the pressure is roughly 250 billion times the air pressure at sea level, and the temperature is about 15 million degrees Celsius. Under that squeeze, hydrogen nuclei slam into each other hard enough to fuse into helium. The helium that comes out weighs very slightly less than the hydrogen that went in, and the missing mass leaves as energy. The sun turns about four million tons of itself into light and heat every second. It has done this for four and a half billion years and has fuel for roughly five billion more. Getting that energy out is slow, ugly work. Above the core sits a layer of gas so dense that light cannot travel straight through it. Energy is swallowed and spat back out, over and over, staggering off in a random direction each time. Tens of thousands of years can pass before it finally reaches the surface. Then it crosses the emptiness to Earth in eight minutes and twenty seconds. The sun is not calm. Its surface is knotted with magnetic fields that twist, snap, and fling clouds of charged particles into space. When one of those clouds strikes Earth's magnetic field, it lights the sky near the poles with auroras. In 1859, an unusually violent one arrived. Telegraph wires sparked, some operators took shocks, and a few machines kept transmitting after their batteries were disconnected. An identical storm today would meet a planet wired end to end with satellites and power grids. Almost every scrap of energy on Earth traces back to that core. Wind blows because sunlight heats some air more than other air. Plants grow by catching photons. Coal and oil are old sunlight, stored by forests that died long before the dinosaurs. Your body is running, right now, on a star.

notes: Helium was found on the sun before it was found on Earth
Named for Helios, the Greek sun
Fraunhofer lines: dark gaps in the solar spectrum
About 73 percent hydrogen, 25 percent helium by mass

blocks.prompt: The Question That Was Supposed to Be Unanswerable
blocks.text: In 1835, a French philosopher named Auguste Comte went looking for the edge of human knowledge. He wanted a clean example of something people would genuinely want to know and could never possibly learn. He chose the stars. We could measure their positions, he wrote, and their distances, and their movements. What they were actually made of would stay permanently beyond us. It was a reasonable thing to say. You cannot collect a sample of a star. He was wrong within his own century, and the star that proved it was the sun. The trick was light itself. Pass sunlight through a prism and it fans out into a band running from red to violet. In the early 1800s, careful observers noticed that the band was not smooth. It was ruled with hundreds of thin dark lines, as though someone had scratched narrow gaps into the light. Nobody knew what they were. By 1859, Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen had worked it out. Every chemical element absorbs light at its own exact set of wavelengths, and no two elements share a set. Heat sodium in a laboratory and it glows at one particular shade of yellow. Look at the sun and there is a dark line sitting at that same yellow, because sodium in the sun's outer gas swallowed that light on its way out. The dark lines are a fingerprint. Comte's impossible question turned out to have an answer, and the answer had been printed in the light falling on his face his entire life. In 1868, during a total eclipse, astronomers found a line in the solar spectrum that matched no element known on Earth. They named the missing substance helium, after Helios, the Greek sun. Nobody isolated it on Earth for another twenty seven years. An element was discovered on a star before any human had held it. What the fingerprints eventually revealed is that the sun is mostly hydrogen, about three quarters of its mass, and nearly all the rest is helium. In the core, at roughly 15 million degrees, hydrogen nuclei are pressed together until they fuse into helium, and each fusion sheds a sliver of mass as energy. The sun converts about four million tons of itself into light every second, and has been doing so for four and a half billion years. That light does not leave in a hurry. A packet of energy born in the core is absorbed and re-emitted so many times by the crushing gas above it that it can take tens of thousands of years to grind its way to the surface. Once free, it crosses 93 million miles of empty space in eight minutes and twenty seconds. The sunlight on your hands is ancient for most of its journey and brand new for the last stretch of it. The sun has not run out of secrets. Its visible surface sits at about 5,500 degrees Celsius, but the thin corona hanging above it exceeds a million. Heat is not supposed to flow from a cooler place to a hotter one, and physicists have been arguing about the corona for more than eighty years. Spacecraft now fly through it to look. Comte drew a line, and the line moved. That is usually what happens to lines like his.
